Mathjax

Math equations can be rendered using Mathjax syntax with AMS symbol support.

Optionally enable this on a per-page basis by adding mathjax: true to your frontmatter.

Then, use $$ ... $$ on a line by itself to render a block equation:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

The raw version is:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

Write in-line equations with \\( ... \\) , like \( x^n / y \) . It’s easy!

Emoji Support

The emojify function can be called directly in templates or Inline Shortcodes.

To enable emoji globally, set enableEmoji to true in your site’s configuration and then you can type emoji shorthand codes directly in content files; e.g.

The Emoji cheat sheet is a useful reference for emoji shorthand codes.

N.B. The above steps enable Unicode Standard emoji characters and sequences in Hugo, however the rendering of these glyphs depends on the browser and the platform. To style the emoji you can either use a third party emoji font or a font stack; e.g.

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}

Why Your “Anonymous” Survey Isn’t Anonymous A data ethics analysis of anonymity, trust, and student survey design

Ever had that weird feeling when a survey says “anonymous” but then asks you to log in?

That happened to me this week while looking at a case study for our Ethics class at Trios College. Students get a link to rate their course. The page says, “All answers will remain anonymous.” But to open it, you must type your college username and password.

Wait… if I log in, how is it anonymous? You know who I am.

That one contradiction is the whole problem.

The Promise vs. The Reality

Let’s break down what is happening.

The survey asks for the course name, not your name, so it tries to look anonymous. But the system already has your login. That’s not anonymous. That’s confidential at best, and even that is broken if management sees the raw file.

In our class we learned the difference:

“Anonymity” = No one can ever link the answer to you. Not even the analyst.

“Confidentiality” = The researcher knows who you are but promises to hide it.

This survey promises the first one but builds the second one. That’s not a small typo. In ethics we call this a failure of Transparency. If you lie to people before they answer, their Informed Consent is not valid. They didn’t agree to the real conditions.

Why Good Intentions Are Not Enough Some people might argue that the survey is still ethical because management’s goal is to improve courses and help students. Improving education is a positive objective, and collecting feedback is often necessary for making informed decisions. However, in data science, good intentions alone are not enough to justify how data is collected. Ethics requires organizations to think about risks before they happen. Even if nobody plans to identify students, the fact that usernames and passwords are required means that identification is possible. Ethical systems should be designed to prevent unnecessary risks rather than relying on promises that data will never be misused. Another issue is trust. Students are more likely to give honest answers when they clearly understand how their information will be used. If they discover later that a supposedly anonymous survey was connected to their login information; they may lose confidence in future surveys and in the organization itself. Trust is difficult to build but very easy to lose. For that reason, ethical data collection is not only about protecting privacy. It is also about maintaining credibility, transparency, and respect for participants. Then there is the question itself: “This course met all of the course objectives. 0-10 Strongly disagree to Strongly agree.”

What does “all” even mean? If 9 out of 10 objectives were great, what number do I click? Only 0 and 10 have labels. This is bad survey design. In data ethics we call this a Data Integrity and Validity problem. Bad questions create bad data, and bad data makes executives make bad decisions about which courses to update.

Three Problems You Don’t See at First

If you look deeper, it gets worse.

• You can still be identified. Even without your name, they have your username + course name + time you submitted. In a small class of 8 students, it’s easy to figure out who gave a low score. We learned this is called Re-identification risk. The fix is De-identification, but they didn’t do it properly. The rule of Data Minimization says: don’t collect a password if you don’t need it for an anonymous survey.

• Students feel pressured. There is a Power Asymmetry here. Students have less power than executive management. Students may believe management or other decision makers have influence over their academic future. If I think my boss can see my honest feedback, I will not be honest. I will give a 9/10 even if the course was a 4/10. That pressure is called Coercion. It doesn’t have to be a threat, just the fear is enough. It ruins the data.

• It can cause real harm. The ethics principle of non-maleficence means “do no harm.” If a student gives honest negative feedback and gets identified, they might feel anxious or fear retaliation. A good data professional following Virtue Ethics would ask, “What would an honest, responsible person do here?” An honest person would not trick students.

So, How Do We Fix It?

If I was the analyst talking to the executives, I wouldn’t just give them charts. I would give them these 5 fixes:

• Remove the login. Use a generic link for each course that doesn’t track who you are. If you need to prevent duplicates, use two separate databases. One that counts who finished, and one that holds answers with no names. • Tell the truth on the consent page. Replace “anonymous” with the truth. Write: “This survey is truly anonymous; we do not track your login. It is voluntary, you can skip any question, and only group averages will be shared with management.” • Fix the questions. Stop using one confusing 0-10 question. Use clear 1-5 scales: 1=Strongly Disagree to 5=Strongly Agree. Ask one thing at a time, not “all objectives.” • Protect small classes. Don’t show individual answers. Only show averages for courses with more than 5 responses. This is called k-anonymity. • Add a data policy. Say who sees the data, how long it is kept, and that passwords are never stored with answers.

These changes are free, fast, and they give you better, more honest data.

What If the Boss Says “Just Do Your Job”?

This is the question everyone in data science faces one day. What if management says, “There are no ethical issues, just give us the insights”?

You still have options. You can be ethical on your side.

First, I would clean the data myself. I would delete usernames, passwords, and timestamps before I do any analysis. I would only give them course averages, never individual rows.

Second, I would write it down. I would send an email documenting my concerns about the false anonymity. That covers Accountability.

Third, if it was serious, I would escalate to a privacy officer or academic integrity office and cite the college’s privacy policy. My loyalty is not just to my boss, but to the students who trusted the system.

You can’t always fix how data was collected, but you can control how you use it.

Final Thought

This assignment taught me that ethics doesn’t start in the code. It starts on the login page.

The real insight for executives is not which course scored 4/10. The real insight is that you will never get the truth if you don’t make people feel safe to tell it.

Promising anonymity while collecting logins breaks trust. And without trust, your data is useless.

As a future data analyst, I learned that my job is not just to produce charts. My job is to protect the people behind the data, even if that means telling management that their system needs to be redesigned before their courses are.
description: A data ethics analysis of anonymity, trust, and student survey design.
title: Why Your Anonymous Survey Isn't Anonymous

Theme Custom Shortcodes

These shortcodes are not Hugo built-ins, but are provided by the theme.

Responsive Images with Cloudinary

You can learn more about this here.

Set the cloudinary_cloud_name parameter in your site config to use this shortcode.

{{< dynamic-img src="/my/image/on/cloudinary" title="A title for the image" >}}

Note that you do not include the file extension (e.g. .png) in the src parameter, as the shortcode will automatically determine the best quality and format for the user’s device.

Optionally, you can customize the general CSS styles for the image:

{{< dynamic-img src="/my/image/on/cloudinary" title="A title for the image" style="max-width:60%" >}}
